interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is pressure growing with depth alone, the same in every tank, so a block's bottom push beats its top push by the weight of liquid displaced, when you drag the probe or block down.
interactive.title: The tank and the probe
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This is a short lesson in sixteen small screens. The main picture is three tanks joined at the bottom. One is narrow, one is wide, and one flares out towards the top. All three are filled to one level, 10 m deep. They are drawn far smaller than life. A pressure probe hangs on a line. It can go down into any tank, from the surface to 10 m. Its gauge reads ρgh. That is the liquid's density × g × the probe's depth below the surface. g is 9.81 newtons for each kilogram. Seawater is 1025 kg/m³. In it, the probe starts at 5 m and reads 1025 × 9.81 × 5, about 50.3 kPa. At 10 m it reads about 100.6 kPa. A thin column above the probe shows the liquid whose weight makes that pressure. At any one depth, the reading is the same in every tank. The joined liquid settles at one level. The probe's face can turn up, sideways or down. The reading stays the same. An absolute switch adds the atmosphere, taken as 100 kPa. Then 5 m reads about 150.3 kPa absolute. A liquid switch swaps seawater for fresh water, at 1000 kg/m³. Then 5 m reads about 49.1 kPa. Then a cube 1 m on a side is lowered into the wide tank. It can be lowered further, and its line holds it there. Arrows on each face grow with depth. The side arrows match in pairs and cancel. Held with its top 2 m down, its top is pushed down with about 20.1 kPa. Its bottom, 3 m down, is pushed up with about 30.2 kPa. On each 1 m² face, that is about 20.1 kN down and about 30.2 kN up. The difference is the upthrust, about 10.1 kN up. A second bar beside it shows the weight of the liquid the cube has pushed aside. That is 1 m³ of liquid, so 1025 kg × 9.81, about 10.1 kN. The two bars match at any depth. A density slider sets the cube's density. It runs from 200 to 1,500 kg/m³ in steps of 25 and starts at 600. The cube's weight is its density × 1 m³ × 9.81. At 600 that is about 5.9 kN. A Let go button releases it. A cube less dense than the liquid rises and floats. It settles where the part below the surface pushes aside its own weight of liquid. That depth is its draught. It equals its density ÷ the liquid's density × 1 m. At 600 it is about 0.59 m in seawater and 0.60 m in fresh water. A mark on the tank wall shows it. At 1025 in seawater, or 1000 in fresh water, it hovers where it is let go. A denser cube sinks to the floor. At 1,500 it weighs about 14.7 kN against an upthrust of about 10.1 kN. Three readouts show the probe pressure, the upthrust and the cube's weight. On a phone they wrap onto two rows. Here it is screen by screen. Screen 1 is a warm-up. A block held under fresh water pushes aside 2 L. A litre of fresh water has a mass of 1 kg. What is the upthrust? The choices are about 19.6 N, about 2 N, or that it depends on what the block is made of. A right answer says Still there. Screen 2 shows the column on a 1 m² patch. ρ is the density. The column weighs ρ × h × 1 m² × g. That weight presses on 1 m², so p = ρgh. Under 10 m of seawater the probe reads about 100.6 kPa, about one atmosphere more. Fresh water is a little less dense, so each metre adds a little less. Screen 3 asks what the probe's gauge reads 5 m down in seawater. The choices are about 50.3 kPa, about 150.3 kPa or about 5.1 kPa. Screen 4 shows the probe at 5 m in each of the three tanks. It fades from one tank to the next. It reads the same in all three. Still water presses too. Screen 5 has two fresh water tanks, each 2 m deep. One has a 0.1 m² base and the other 10 m². What pressure is on each bottom? The choices are about 19.6 kPa on both, 100 times more on the wide one, or more on the narrow one. Screen 6 turns the probe's face up, sideways and down at 3 m in seawater. It reads about 30.2 kPa each way. Then the screen shows the absolute switch, as with the air receiver. Screen 7 has a small plate 3 m down in seawater. Facing up, it reads about 30.2 kPa. Turned to face sideways, does it read about 30.2 kPa, 0 kPa or about 15.1 kPa? Screen 8 shows a hydraulic jack. Two cylinders of oil are joined at the bottom, each under a piston. 100 N pushes down on a 10 cm² piston. That is 100 N ÷ 0.001 m², or 100 kPa, everywhere in the oil. On the 200 cm² piston it lifts 2,000 N. The small piston goes down 20 cm while the load rises 1 cm. Work in, 100 N × 0.2 m, is 20 J. Work out, 2,000 N × 0.01 m, is also 20 J. Screen 9 has a jack with a 5 cm² piston and a 300 cm² piston. A push of 60 N goes on the small one. What load can the big one lift? The choices are 60 N, 3,600 N or 1 N. Screen 10 shows the cube held under, with its arrows and the two matching bars. The extra pressure on its bottom is ρg × 1 m, acting on 1 m². So the upthrust is ρg × 1 m³. That is the weight of 1 m³ of seawater, 1025 kg, about 10.1 kN. On screen 11, the cube is pushed down until its top is 6 m deep. Its top now feels about 60.3 kPa. Its bottom feels about 70.4 kPa. What is the upthrust? The choices are about 10.1 kN, about 30.2 kN or about 70.4 kN. Screen 12 lets go of a cube of 1,500 kg/m³, and it sinks. It gives relative density, a density ÷ fresh water's. Seawater's is 1.025. A steel hull floats because its mass ÷ all the space its outside encloses is less than the water's density. Screen 13 lets go of a cube of 600 kg/m³, and it rises to float. It must push aside 600 kg of seawater, 600 ÷ 1025, about 0.59 m³. On its 1 m² base, that is a draught of 0.59 m. In fresh water it is 0.60 m. On screen 14, a box-shaped pontoon 4 m by 2 m has a mass of 4,000 kg. How deep does it sit in seawater? The choices are about 0.49 m, about 0.50 m or about 0.98 m. Screens 15 and 16 mix it all. On screen 15, a sensor sits 20 m down in seawater. What absolute pressure does it feel? The choices are about 301 kPa, about 201 kPa or about 296 kPa. On screen 16, a sealed float of 1 m³ is weighted to hover in seawater. So its mass is 1025 kg. Moved into fresh water, does it sink, float higher or still hover? It sinks. The 1 m³ of fresh water it pushes aside weighs about 9.8 kN. That is less than its own weight of about 10.1 kN. Where it can be, a wrong pick is drawn on the picture. That way you see where it fails.
interactive.ignores: The tanks are drawn far smaller than 10 m. The cube is drawn to the same scale. The liquid is still. Its density is taken as the same from top to bottom. Real seawater's density varies a little with its temperature, saltiness and depth. g is taken as 9.81 everywhere. The atmosphere is taken as 100 kPa, though it changes with the weather. The cube floats level and upright. Whether a real floating body stays upright is its stability. That is a separate question, not shown here. Liquid always reaches under the cube. A cube sealed flat against a floor has no liquid beneath it. It loses the push on its bottom. Surface tension is left out. It is what lets very small, light things rest on water. The jack's pistons are level with each other and slide without friction. Its oil is taken as not squeezing at all.

explain.text:
Still liquid presses on everything in it. It presses harder the deeper you go. The reason is weight. The pressure at any depth comes from the weight of the liquid above it. Picture a column of liquid standing on a patch of 1 m². It reaches up to the surface. Its height is the depth, h, so its volume is h × 1 m². Its mass is that volume times the liquid's [[density]], which is its mass per cubic metre. Its weight is that mass times g, 9.81 newtons for each kilogram. All that weight rests on the 1 m² patch. So the pressure there is density × g × depth. It is written p = ρgh. Here ρ, the Greek letter rho, stands for the density. A liquid barely squeezes. So its density is near enough the same all the way down. That is why each metre adds the same pressure. Seawater's density is about 1025 kg/m³.[^2] So 10 m of it adds 1025 × 9.81 × 10, about 100.6 kPa. That is about as much again as the whole atmosphere.[^1] With the surface open to the air, a gauge reads that ρgh. For the absolute pressure, add the atmosphere's 100 kPa, as with gases.

Look at what ρgh leaves out. The tank's width is not in it. Nor is its shape. Join a narrow tank, a wide one and a flaring one at the bottom. Then fill them. The liquid settles at one level in all three. At any one depth, the probe reads the same in each. If one tank's bottom pressed harder, it would push liquid through the join until the levels matched. In the flaring tank, the sloping walls hold up the extra liquid's weight. At any point, the pressure pushes every way at once. It pushes square to whatever surface it meets. It needs no movement, either. Still water presses because it has weight.

Now shut a liquid in. Push on it anywhere, and its pressure rises by the same amount everywhere. That is [[Pascal's principle]]. A hydraulic jack uses it. Push 100 N on a 10 cm² piston. That is 100 N ÷ 0.001 m², or 100 kPa. The same 100 kPa acts on a 200 cm² piston, so it lifts 2,000 N. Nothing comes free, though. The small piston must move 20 times as far. Push it down 20 cm, and the load rises 1 cm. Work in is 100 N × 0.2 m, or 20 J. Work out is 2,000 N × 0.01 m, also 20 J.

Now hold a cube 1 m on a side under seawater, with its top 2 m down. The pushes on its sides match in pairs, so they cancel. Its top is pushed down by about 20.1 kPa. Its bottom is 3 m down, so it is pushed up by about 30.2 kPa. On each 1 m² face, the bottom wins by about 10.1 kN. That net push up is the [[upthrust]]. The extra pressure at the bottom is ρg × the cube's height. It acts on the bottom's area. Height × area is the cube's volume, so the upthrust is ρg × that volume. That is the weight of the seawater the cube has pushed aside. So an object partly or wholly in a liquid feels an upthrust equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces.[^4] Push the cube deeper and both pushes grow by the same amount. So the upthrust stays the same. What the cube is made of does not change it either.

Whether it floats is a contest between its weight and the upthrust. Its weight depends on its own density. The upthrust depends on the liquid's. A cube less dense than the liquid rises. As it comes out of the surface, it displaces less. So the upthrust falls. It settles where the upthrust equals its weight. Its [[draught]] is the depth of its bottom below the surface. Take a 1 m cube with a density of 600 kg/m³. Its mass is 600 kg, so it weighs about 5.9 kN. It must push aside 600 kg of seawater. That is 600 ÷ 1025, about 0.59 m³. On its 1 m² base, that is a draught of about 0.59 m. Fresh water is less dense, about 1000 kg/m³. So the same cube sits deeper, at 0.60 m. A thing's [[relative density]] is its density ÷ fresh water's. Seawater's is about 1.025. A cube exactly as dense as the liquid hovers. A denser one sinks. So size or weight alone does not decide it. Think of all the space a steel hull's outside encloses. The hull floats because its mass is less than the mass of water that would fill that space.

**In a still liquid, pressure grows with depth as ρgh. The extra push under an object is an upthrust equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces.**

analogy.text: Think of cells in series in a battery. Each cell adds its own voltage, whatever its size. A big cell and a small one of the same kind give the same volts. The big one can just deliver far more charge. Each metre of liquid adds the same pressure, whatever the tank's width. The width sets the total push on the bottom, as a cell's size sets its charge. It does not set the pressure.
analogy.breaks: A cell makes its voltage by chemistry. That voltage drives current one way round a circuit. In a still liquid, the pressure from depth comes only from the weight of the liquid above. It pushes every way at once. That sideways and upward push is what makes upthrust. Nothing in a battery pushes up on anything.

practice.text:
**Safe first:** Before you open a cover or pipe joint below a liquid's level, isolate it from every pressure source, such as a pump. Then drain the liquid down past it. The liquid above pushes on it with at least its ρgh. Last, confirm zero pressure at an open vent or needle valve before you break in.[^5]

**Pressure at a depth**
- Measure the depth straight down from the liquid's surface. Along a sloping pipe, only the height counts.
- With the surface open to the air, the gauge pressure in Pa is density × 9.81 × depth.
- For absolute pressure, add the atmosphere, about 100 kPa.
- For the push on a level plate, multiply that pressure by the plate's area.

**Force through a jack**
- Pressure = force ÷ area. Change cm² to m² first: 1 cm² is 0.0001 m².
- The oil passes that pressure on to the other piston. Its force is the pressure × its own area.
- The bigger force moves the shorter distance. Work in equals work out, less friction.

**Will it float, and how deep?**
- Find its overall density. That is its mass ÷ all the space its outside encloses.
- If it is less dense than the liquid, it floats. If it is denser, it sinks.
- Its relative density is its density ÷ fresh water's. Above 1, it sinks in fresh water.
- For a box with straight sides and a flat bottom, draught = mass ÷ (liquid's density × length × breadth).

**Rules of thumb:** Each metre of seawater adds about 10 kPa. So 10 m adds about one atmosphere. A floating thing sits a little deeper in fresh water than in seawater.

**Worked example:** A box-shaped pontoon 4 m by 2 m has a mass of 4,000 kg. In seawater, its draught is 4,000 ÷ (1025 × 4 × 2), about 0.49 m. In fresh water it is 4,000 ÷ (1000 × 8) = 0.50 m. A level plate of 0.5 m² sits 3 m down in seawater. The pressure there is 1025 × 9.81 × 3, about 30.2 kPa gauge. The push on it is 30.2 kPa × 0.5 m², about 15.1 kN.

**Common mistakes**
- Using the tank's width or volume. In a still, open tank, only the depth sets the pressure.
- Measuring the depth along a slope instead of straight down.
- Mixing gauge and absolute. A gauge leaves out the atmosphere.
- Passing the force through a jack, not the pressure.
- Forgetting g. A kilogram is a mass. Its weight is 9.81 N.
- Using fresh water's density for seawater, or the other way round.
- Judging floating by size or weight alone. What decides it is the object's density against the liquid's.
